| | Week 1: developed market | Week 2: emerging market |
|:-------|:----------------|:----------------|
| Data | 2021–24, 163,150 claims; 626,639 rows to price | 2023–24, 9,258 claims; 209,063 rows to price |
| Submitted file | six-expert geometric mean, recalibrated per line | v13: ensemble ranking with segment levels read from the leaderboard |
| Public / private D² | 0.12851 / **0.13830** | **0.17172** / pending (v12, public 0.17095, also selected) |

The score is the Tweedie deviance D² with power 1.5 over all rows of the three lines. My first
Week 2 file, a plain LightGBM, scored 0.12519. Three ideas carried the work: get the target right
before modelling; in a new market, start from what the old market knows and learn only the
differences; and keep the level of a segment apart from the ranking inside it, because the 2025
book is too unlike the training years for a back-test to judge levels.

# Data and target

Each week runs the same three scripts (read, clean, build features), each with an executed
notebook as evidence. Every fix is logged with the rows it changed. No row is dropped and nothing
is imputed. Among the issues found: customer ids that had lost their leading zeros (123,664 rows);
exposure recorded in days or on a 360-day basis (13,880 + 595 rows); sums insured in units instead
of thousands (3,527 + 349); a case reserve typed with an extra digit (11.9m for 1.19m); impossible
years licensed, restored from the same policy's other years (3,717); and 604 claims stored twice
under a second id, which inflated 2022 claim counts by 1.4%.

**Target.** The ultimate cost of the claims whose loss date falls in the row's period, net of excess
and recoveries, repudiated claims excluded. Claims are valued at 31 December 2024, so 2024 is not
fully reported (about half of its bodily-injury cost is in). Every model's offset is
log(exposure × share of claims reported), from a reporting pattern per peril. Open claims are
developed with the recovery ratio of closed ones, costs are trended to 2025 per peril, and costs
above the 99.5% quantile are capped and returned as a load per line (1.02 to 1.06).

**Feature selection.** A column is kept only if it beats 20 random "probe" columns out of time,
alone and inside a small LightGBM, with a pass mark that lets at most 1 in 20 noise columns through.
Week 1 keeps 53 / 44 / 49 features (motor / buildings / contents), Week 2 only 28 / 14 / 9: two years
of a small book cannot prove weaker effects.

# Week 1: six experts and a geometric mean

For each line, six experts are each trained three times: on 2021–22 to price 2023, on 2021–23 to
price 2024, and on every year to price 2025. All are LightGBM with an exact log offset, except the GLM.

| Expert | What it models |
|:-------|:----------------------------|
| `total` | Tweedie GBM on capped total cost, times the line's large-loss load |
| `glm` | Tweedie GLM on banded numeric factors and grouped categories |
| `peril` | one Tweedie GBM per peril, with its own reporting share and load, summed |
| `fs_gamma`, `fs_lognorm` | Poisson frequency × claim size (Gamma; or lognormal with a risk-specific variance) |
| `fs_peril` | frequency × claim size for each peril, summed |

The predictions are combined row by row with an equal-weight geometric mean, then recalibrated per
line with a two-parameter Tweedie GLM, $\log E = \log(\text{exposure}\cdot L) + b_0 + b_1 \log(\text{geo}/L)$,
where $L$ is the line's mean rate. It is fitted on the two back-test years ($b_1$ = 1.04 motor,
1.10 buildings, 1.09 contents).

| Back-test D², all lines (calibration fitted on the other year) | 2023 | 2024 |
|:----------------------------|------:|------:|
| one LightGBM on total cost | 0.1364 | 0.1338 |
| best single expert (`fs_peril`) | 0.1379 | 0.1365 |
| geometric mean of the six, recalibrated | **0.1386** | **0.1375** |

Frequency × claim-size experts beat a single cost model in every line and year, and the six together
beat each of them. A seventh expert (a claim-size mixture of experts) gave the same private score,
so I kept the simpler file. The table comes from the rebuilt pipeline. The submitted file came
from the 22 October code, which reported 0.1380 / 0.1367 and predates the duplicate-claim and
years-licensed fixes. Its 2025 predictions have a log correlation of 0.996 to 0.998 with the rebuild.

# Week 2: adapting to the emerging market

The new market broke most of what Week 1 could take for granted:

| | Week 1 | Week 2 |
|:--------|:----------|:------------------|
| History | 4 years, 163k claims | 2 years, 9k claims (about 1,000 per home line) |
| New business in the year priced | close to the training mix | 77% of 2025, against 12–15% of training rows |
| Gender | not a rating factor | a permitted rating factor |
| Weather of the year | inside the training range | 2025 far outside it (rainfall anomaly −128 mm against ±3 mm) |
| Buildings experience | stable | 2023 fire-cost spike: 2024 came in at 0.59 of 2023's prediction |

**Transfer from the developed market.** A LightGBM is fitted on every Week 1 row with only the
factors that mean the same thing in both markets (30 motor, 24 buildings, 26 contents), always
including renewal count, and its log rate goes into the offset of the Week 2 models. The local trees
then learn only how this market differs, and need just 20 to 110 trees. Each Week 1 expert is rebuilt
on a prior of its own component (frequency, claim size, each peril). A peril with fewer than 50
claims (300 for claim sizes) uses its prior alone, re-levelled. This-year weather is dropped.

**Choices made by cross-validation** (five folds of customers over 2023–24, since two years give
only one forward test): one-split trees for motor and contents; a strong GLM ridge (a weak one
overfits buildings below D² = 0); a member set per line instead of all six (motor `total` +
`fs_peril` + `glm`, buildings `fs_lognorm` + `peril`, contents `total` + `glm`), because two years
hold too few claims to learn claim sizes; and a recalibration slope fixed at 1, since a fitted slope
did not carry from one year to the other. New-business and gender factors are measured on
out-of-fold predictions and shrunk towards no effect.

| Forward test: fit on 2023, score 2024, all lines | D² |
|:----------------------------|------:|
| LightGBM on Week 2 data only | 0.1026 |
| developed-market prior alone | 0.1259 |
| LightGBM on top of the prior | 0.1277 |
| ensemble on priors | **0.1300** |

# What the leaderboard taught me

The ensemble (v4) scored 0.16198 in public, below my earlier single transfer LightGBM (0.16529),
although it ranked the 2024 risks better. The difference was in the levels. The 2024 back-test is
13% new business and 2025 is 77%, so the back-test can judge the ranking inside a segment but not
the level of new business, buildings or gender.

So I split the problem. **Ranking.** v5 keeps the earlier file's total in each of ten segments
(line × new business × gender) and replaces the ranking inside them with a 50/50 geometric blend
with my ensemble. On 2024 rows weighted to the 2025 mix it ranks better (within-segment D² 0.1067
against 0.1016). It scored exactly 0.16529: the public score barely reacts to ranking inside segments.

**Levels.** For Tweedie p = 1.5, multiplying a segment's predictions by $c$ changes the deviance by
exactly
$$\Delta D = 4\left[(c^{-1/2}-1)A + (c^{1/2}-1)B\right], \qquad A=\textstyle\sum y\,\mu^{-1/2},\quad B=\sum \mu^{1/2},$$
so the best level is $c^* = A/B$, and any scored file that differs from another only by segment
factors measures it. One model, linear in the ten best levels, fits 13 public scores within 0.0001.
Five of them, left out of the fit, were predicted up to one constant offset. It showed that motor
needed a much wider gender split than any model of 2023–24 gave: new-business men about ×1.37 on
v5, women about ×0.97 (@fig-levels).

**Luck.** The public score covers only a sample of 2025 rows, so a segment's best level on it is off
by $\text{sd} = \sqrt{\phi / (\text{share}\cdot\sum\mu^{1/2})}$: 8% for motor new-business men, 13%
for buildings new business and 24% for buildings renewals at a 30% public share. The model fits that
luck separately and gives two answers: the best levels for the public rows (v13) and the best levels
for rows not yet scored (v12), which pulls the noisy segments back towards v5.

v12 scored 0.17095 (expected 0.1708) and v13 0.17172 (expected 0.1714). Against v5, the model
expects v12 to gain 0.0042 on unseen rows and v13 0.0037 (sd about 0.0015). On Kaggle I selected
both: v12 is my best estimate for the final ranking, and v13 wins only if the true levels are as
extreme as the public rows suggest. The Week 2 file submitted here is v13, my best score. Two last
ranking changes (no this-year weather in the buildings and contents model, motor spread ×1.05)
scored 0.17032 (v14): 0.0006 below v12, with a public-luck sd of 0.0008. The leaderboard cannot
read that either way, so v14 was not selected.

**In short, what the new market changed.** (1) I stopped learning everything locally: the
developed market supplies the relativities and the emerging data only corrects them. (2) Simpler
local models won: one-split trees, a strong ridge, fewer experts, no fitted slope. (3) The back-test
was no longer enough, because 2025 is mostly new business, so ranking and level were judged on
different evidence. (4) The public leaderboard became a noisy measurement to model, not a score to
maximise.

# Major decisions

| Decision | Rejected | Evidence |
|:-------------------|:-----------|:--------------|
| Fix data errors with evidence; drop and impute nothing | dropping or imputing rows | cleaning log per round |
| Geometric mean of experts, recalibrated per line (Week 1) | one LightGBM | +0.0022 (2023) and +0.0037 (2024) back-test D² |
| Developed-market prior in the offset (Week 2) | Week 2-only models | +0.025 forward D² |
| Members per line by cross-validation; slope fixed at 1 | all six experts; fitted slope | contents: all six 0.1071 against `total` alone 0.1087 |
| Segment levels kept apart from ranking | trusting the back-test's levels | v4 0.16198 against v5 0.16529 |
| Aim at unseen rows, not the public sample | chasing the public score | public luck sd 8–24% per segment |

# Use of AI

I worked alone, with an AI coding agent (Claude Code in VS Code) as the partner at every step. The
agent wrote and ran most of the code and drafted this write-up. The questions, the direction and
every decision to implement stayed with me.

* **Prompting to explore ideas.** Most of the work was a long series of prompts that proposed and
  tested ideas: the developed-market prior, the expert ensembles, segment-level probes, the
  public-luck model. Each idea became a script and was measured out of time before it counted.
* **Context to point the search.** Each prompt came with context: the case study, what had already
  been tried and why it failed (kept in `KNOWLEDGE.md`), and the question to answer. That kept the
  agent exploring in the direction I chose instead of starting over or repeating dead ends.
* **Skills for coding and best practice.** Two project skills in the repository
  (`.claude/skills/data-scientist`, `ml-engineer`) set how the agent works: frame the problem
  first, test out of time, distrust its own gains, keep code reproducible and versioned.
* **Every idea questioned independently.** A result was not accepted from the run that produced
  it. Each idea was questioned separately, so the agent had to check its own work. Factor searches
  looked strong when the same two years chose and scored them; a permutation test then showed real
  factors pass no more often than shuffled ones, so only gender was kept. A review after the Week 1
  deadline found a sign error in the contents frequency trend; it is documented, kept in the code
  that reproduces the submitted file, and fixed in the rebuild.
* **Human sign-off before implementation.** Nothing went into the pipeline or a submission until I
  had reviewed the plan and its evidence. I chose the target definition, what evidence counts,
  which files to submit and select, and when to stop probing the leaderboard.

# Assumptions

* 2025 claims follow 2023–24 after trend (motor severity 0–7.9% a year by peril, buildings severity
  6%, contents frequency 1.4% and severity 3.4%). Reporting patterns are stable, and open claims
  develop like closed ones.
* For factors defined the same way in both markets, the developed market's relativities are a sound
  starting point. The emerging market differs in level and in a few effects that local models can learn.
* Public-leaderboard rows are a random sample of 2025 (about 30%). The order of v12 and v13 holds
  for any share from 20% to 50%.
* Gender is a permitted rating factor in the emerging market, as the case study states.

# Limitations

* Two years of emerging-market data, and buildings is lumpy: a few large claims decide its public
  score, and its levels carry 8–10% uncertainty.
* Week 2 levels rest partly on the public leaderboard. That is allowed in the competition, but in
  practice it amounts to calibrating on a sample of the book's own outcomes, and the bands in
  @fig-levels are wide.
* Back-tests cannot judge new-business levels, and ranking changes such as v14 are smaller than
  the public score's noise.
* The submitted Week 1 file keeps the contents trend sign error. The per-line recalibration absorbs
  most of it (intercept about +10%), but contents relativities may be slightly off.

# Guardrails

* **Leakage.** Outcome-driven columns are excluded: `renewal_decision`, and
  `customer_service_contacts` (zero on 0.2% of rows with a claim, against 67% without). Claims
  history is built as known on 1 January of each year.
* **Governance.** The written premium is excluded (a model using it would copy the old tariff), as
  are marketing and service fields and personal data such as surname. Gender is used only where
  permitted, and its factor moves price between men and women without changing the line's total.
* **Evidence before every submission.** Each file is tested out of time first, then registered as a
  new version with its evidence, description and checksum. Versions are never overwritten.
* **File checks.** A file is saved only with one row per sample row id, in order, every prediction
  finite and positive. The Week 1 code adds block and escalate rules: back-test D² ≤ 0 blocks; A/E
  outside 1 ± 5%, feature drift (PSI ≥ 0.25) or a pure-premium shift above 15% against history goes
  to actuarial sign-off.
* **Noise control.** Probe columns in feature selection, permutation tests on factor searches, and
  the public-luck model all guard against fitting noise, including noise an AI agent would report as a gain.
* **Reproducibility.** Every step is a script under git. The data steps give the same bytes on every
  run, and the Week 1 file rebuilds from cached expert predictions in a minute (largest relative
  difference 2e-15).
